title: Rehat as love
hook: rules kept from love, not fear

segments.voice: Yesterday, faithfulness in marriage: one light in two bodies. Your line was faithful. Which small promise at home did you keep? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

Every evening, in one house, a teenager practices a piano piece because a parent is standing in the doorway with a timer. In the house next door, another teenager practices the same piece because she heard it once on a rainy afternoon and can't get it out of her head. From the hallway, the two sound almost the same. Same scales, same wrong notes, same hour. But ask each of them in ten years whether they still play, and you'll likely hear two very different answers. This whole block has been a reading of a code: what to wear, what to say each morning, what to refuse. A list like that can be kept the first way, with someone standing in the doorway. Today asks whether the Gurus meant it to be kept the second way.
screen: `TWO STUDENTS, ONE PIECE.` → `ONE HAS A TIMER IN THE DOORWAY.` → `ONE CAN'T GET THE TUNE OUT OF HER HEAD.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Japji, at its twenty-first step, on Ang 4. Guru Nanak names three things together: hearing, believing, and holding love in the mind. In paraphrase, the one who hears, accepts and loves bathes at a shrine deep inside. The order matters. Hearing comes first, and love is where it lands. Then a line from Guru Nanak on Ang 1412, in paraphrase: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm. That is not a soft line. It asks for everything. But it calls the asking a game of love. It doesn't call it a duty roster. Now, honesty: the Gurus also speak of bhau, a word for fear, or awe, of God, and the Japji itself talks about it. Some readers hear awe in it more than terror, the feeling of standing before something vast. And love and awe sit side by side in the hymns, without one canceling the other. But it's love the Gurus call a game, and love they ask to be played. So read the rehat that way. The kesh, the morning banis, the clear mind, faithfulness at home: they can be kept with someone standing in the doorway, a parent, a community, a worry about what people will say. Or they can be kept the way the second student plays, because the tune is already inside. The code itself can't tell the difference from the hallway. Only the one keeping it knows which kind of keeping it is.
screen: `ANG 4: HEARING, BELIEVING, LOVING.` · `ANG 1412: THE GAME OF LOVE.` · `BHAU: AWE BESIDE LOVE.` · then, large: `THE SAME RULE, KEPT TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one rule gladly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one rule you already keep, any kind: a habit, a promise, a practice, a line you won't cross. Ask, gently, why you keep it. Is someone standing in the doorway? Or is there a tune you love underneath it? There's no wrong answer. Then, for the rest of the sit, try holding that rule as something you'd choose again today. Let the breath be easy. The bell holds the time.
Rehat as love. The Gurus put love at the end of hearing and believing, and call the whole path a game of love. The rules can be kept from fear or from love; the hymns point to love. Today's word.
Your line: kept in love. Today, when you do one ordinary duty, a chore, a call, a habit, try doing it for the person or the thing you love underneath it. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

notes: Japji pauri 21 (Ang 4): 'suniaa manniaa man keetaa bhaao' paraphrased as hearing, believing (accepting), holding love in the mind, and the inner shrine bath. Please confirm.
Ang 1412: Guru Nanak's 'jau tau prem khelan ka chaao' paraphrased; please confirm Ang and wording.

The note on bhau (fear/awe) and bhaau (love) as distinct Gurmukhi words: 'some readers hear awe more than terror' is attributed; please confirm. The trapdoor's third floor depends on the two words being distinct (ਭਉ / ਭਾਉ); please confirm spelling and transliteration.
